28103.etyen:
From an altered, euphemistic pronunciation of Jesus (“Jesus”).
The underlying name ultimately derives from Latin Iēsūs (“Jesus”), from Ancient Greek Ἰησοῦς (Iēsoûs, “Jesus; Joshua”), representing Aramaic יֵשׁוּע (“Yeshua”), corresponding to Biblical Hebrew יֵשׁוּעַ (“Yeshua, Jeshua”). This is a shortened form of Biblical Hebrew יְהוֹשֻׁעַ (“Joshua”), traditionally interpreted as “Yahweh is salvation”.
The expression (i) jøsse navn represents i (“in”) + Jesu (“of Jesus”) + navn (“name”), literally “in Jesus' name”.
Compare Norwegian Nynorsk jøss and jøsses, Danish jøsses (“gosh, goodness”), and

1003207.etyen:
Internationalism, from Swazi eSwatini, the native Swazi name, a locative formation meaning “land of the Swazis”. The name is based on the ethnonym Swati, which derives from the name of Mswati II; the native form contains the locative elements e- … -ini.
Compare Danish Eswatini, Swedish Eswatini, German Eswatini and English Eswatini.

Last part from Old Norse grár (“grey, spiteful”), from Proto-Germanic *grēwaz (“grey”), from Proto-Indo-European *ǵʰreh₁- (“to grow (of plants)”).

1004487.etyen:
From Latin Otilia, originally Odilia, a Latinised form of Old High German Odila and Otila, pet forms of names such as Oda. The Old High German names are formed from the Germanic name element reflected in *audaz (“wealth, riches”), with a pet-name or diminutive ending.
Compare Danish Otilia, Swedish Otilia, German Ottilie and English Ottilie (“female given name”).

en.g: Used to form patronymic and matronymic names from given names, meaning “daughter of”

1004743.etyen:
Inherited from Old Norse dóttir (“daughter”), also reflected in the independent noun datter (“daughter”); used as the final element of patronymics and matronymics.
Compare Norwegian Nynorsk -dotter, Danish -datter, Swedish -dotter, Icelandic -dóttir and Faroese -dóttir (“patronymic or matronymic suffix meaning “daughter of””).

en.g: butter tub; a traditional lidded wooden stave container used for storing or transporting butter
x: Smøret ble lagt i en smørambar før det skulle fraktes.
The butter was placed in a butter tub before it was transported.
Sivert kom ind med en Smøramber i Haanden.
Sivert came in with a butter tub in his hand.

1004999.etyen:
PIE word
 *smérus
 PIE word
 *h₂m̥bʰi
Compound of smør (“butter”) + ambar (“wooden pail, wooden container”), literally “butter ambar”. The first element ultimately continues Proto-Germanic *smerwą (“grease, butter, fat”), from Proto-Indo-European *smérus (“grease, fat”). The second element derives through Middle Low German from Latin amphora (“two-handled jar, amphora”), ultimately from Ancient Greek elements meaning “on both sides” and “bearer”, the latter from *bʰer- (“to carry, bear”); see ambar.
